title: Causal Effect Estimation under Informative Censoring: A Multiple-Imputation Approach with Shadow Calibration

problem.claim: Causal effects on time-to-event outcomes must be estimated when outcomes are right-censored and the censoring mechanism is linked to event time.

gap.claim: Informative censoring violates conventional non-informative-censoring assumptions and causes unresolved bias in causal effect estimation.

contributions.claim: A theoretical framework is established for identifying causal effects on time-to-event outcomes under informative censoring.
MISC uses fully observed shadow variables to support imputation of censored event times and causal effect estimation.

author_reported_evidence.claim: On semi-synthetic benchmarks and real-world medical and e-commerce datasets, the authors report state-of-the-art performance for causal effect estimation and counterfactual prediction.
The authors report that code is available in a public repository.

narrative_sequence.summary: Accurate causal effect estimation is important for time-to-event outcomes.
Right-censoring is often informative, violating conventional survival-analysis assumptions and creating censoring bias.
The paper presents an identification framework and the MISC method based on learned shadow representations and multiple imputation.
Experiments are reported on semi-synthetic and real-world datasets from medical and e-commerce settings.

source_observation.claim: Censoring related to event time can make latent information in censored observations non-ignorable for causal estimation.

interpretation.claim: Methods that assume non-informative censoring may be biased when the observation process depends on the outcome time.

application.claim: When estimating causal effects with time-to-event data, model or assess the censoring mechanism and consider auxiliary covariates related to event time.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish when the proposed shadow-variable conditions hold in other datasets or applications.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the identification assumptions or theoretical conditions in detail.
The abstract does not report dataset sizes, baselines, metrics, or numerical results.
The abstract does not establish independent verification of the reported performance.
